records.source: וַיַּעֲשׂ֧וּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל הָרַ֖ע בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַיִּתְּנֵ֧ם יְהוָ֛ה בְּיַד־מִדְיָ֖ן שֶׁ֥בַע שָׁנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And did [the] sons of Israel the evil in [the] eyes of Yahweh, and gave them Yahweh into [the] hand of Midian seven years.
pieces: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} did what was evil in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave them into the power of Midian for seven years.

L.1: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel did the evil in [the] eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave them into [the] hand of Midian seven years.

R.1: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said was evil. So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} handed them over to the Midianites for seven years.

decisions.choice: the pattern of Judges begins again: Israel does evil, and Yahweh hands them over
decisions.reason: This is the fourth turn of the cycle described in 2:11-19 (3:7-8, 12; 4:1-2). After the forty years of peace that followed Deborah's victory (5:31), Israel again turns away, and Yahweh gives them into the power of an enemy.

decisions.choice: gave them into the hand of Midian: put them under Midian's power
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power and control. Yahweh lets Midian overpower Israel; the same picture returns in verses 2, 9, 13 and 14.

decisions.choice: Midian: a people of the desert regions east and south of Israel
decisions.reason: The Midianites were traced back to Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2). They lived as herders and traders, and they had joined Moab against Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 22:4; 25:6-18; 31:1-12).

decisions.choice: gave them into the power of (Balanced); handed them over to (Readable)
decisions.reason: As with "sold them into the hand of" elsewhere in Judges, Balanced turns "hand" into "power" and Readable says "handed them over". Readable names the people, "the Midianites", for the nation "Midian".

records.heading: Midian oppresses Israel

records.source: וַתָּ֥עָז יַד־מִדְיָ֖ן עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מִפְּנֵ֨י מִדְיָ֜ן עָשֽׂוּ לָהֶ֣ם׀בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֶת־הַמִּנְהָרוֹת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בֶּֽהָרִ֔ים וְאֶת־הַמְּעָר֖וֹת וְאֶת־הַמְּצָדֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And prevailed [the] hand of Midian over Israel; because of Midian made for themselves [the] sons of Israel the dens which [are] in the mountains, and the caves, and the strongholds.
pieces: Midian's power weighed heavily on Israel. Because of Midian, the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} made themselves the hiding places in the mountains, and the caves and the strongholds.

L.2: And the hand of Midian prevailed over Israel. Because of Midian the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel made for themselves the dens that [are] in the mountains, and the caves, and the strongholds.

R.2: The Midianites had so much power over Israel that the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} made hiding places for themselves in the hills. They also used caves and places that were hard to reach.

decisions.choice: dens: shelters cut or dug into the hillsides, perhaps clefts in the rock
decisions.reason: The word appears only here in the Bible, so its exact sense is not certain. It comes from a word family linked with light or with channels, and may name holes or crevices in the rock that let in light, or tunnels dug as hiding places. The context makes clear that they were places to hide from the raiders.

decisions.choice: strongholds: high places that are hard to reach
decisions.reason: The word is used of rugged heights where people could hold out against attackers, as David did in the strongholds of the wilderness (1 Samuel 23:14).

decisions.choice: the dens, the caves, the strongholds: places the first readers knew
decisions.reason: Each noun has the article, as if the writer is pointing to hiding places that were still known in the hills in his own day.

decisions.choice: places that were hard to reach
decisions.reason: Readable explains "strongholds" by what made them useful: attackers could not easily get to them.

records.source: וְהָיָ֖ה אִם־זָרַ֣ע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְעָלָ֨ה מִדְיָ֧ן וַֽעֲמָלֵ֛ק וּבְנֵי־קֶ֖דֶם וְעָל֥וּ עָלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And it was, whenever sowed Israel, then came up Midian and Amalek and [the] sons of [the] east, and they came up against him.
pieces: Whenever Israel had sown its crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the peoples of the east would come up and attack them.

L.3: And it would be, whenever Israel had sown, Midian and Amalek and the {{gender:people|sons}} of the east would come up, and they would come up against them.

R.3: Every time the Israelites planted their crops, the Midianites came up to attack them. The Amalekites and other people from the east came with them.

decisions.choice: would come up: something that happened again and again
decisions.reason: The verb forms describe a repeated pattern, not a single raid. Every year, after Israel had sown, the raiders came back at harvest time to take the crops.

decisions.choice: Amalek and the people of the east: other desert peoples who joined Midian
decisions.reason: Amalek was Israel's old enemy from the wilderness (Exodus 17:8-16; 3:13 in this book). "The people of the east" is a broad name for the tribes of the desert east of the Jordan (Genesis 29:1; Job 1:3).

decisions.choice: against him: against Israel as one people
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "against him", treating Israel as a single person, as in the first half of the verse ("Israel sowed").

decisions.choice: them
decisions.reason: English uses "them" for the nation, since "him" would sound like one man.

records.source: וַיַּחֲנ֣וּ עֲלֵיהֶ֗ם וַיַּשְׁחִ֨יתוּ֙ אֶת־יְב֣וּל הָאָ֔רֶץ עַד־בּוֹאֲךָ֖ עַזָּ֑ה וְלֹֽא־יַשְׁאִ֤ירוּ מִֽחְיָה֙ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְשֶׂ֥ה וָשׁ֖וֹר וַחֲמֽוֹר׃
records.gloss: And they camped against them and destroyed [the] produce of the land as far as your coming to Gaza, and not they left sustenance in Israel, and sheep and ox and donkey.
pieces: They would camp on their land and ruin the crops all the way to Gaza. They left nothing in Israel to live on, not a sheep, an ox or a donkey.

L.4: And they camped against them and destroyed the produce of the land as far as your coming to Gaza, and they did not leave sustenance in Israel, or sheep or ox or donkey.

R.4: They set up camp on the Israelites' land and ruined the crops as far as the city of Gaza. They left the Israelites nothing to eat, and no sheep, cattle or donkeys.

decisions.choice: as far as your coming to Gaza: all the way to Gaza
decisions.reason: "As you come to" is a common way of giving a distance (Genesis 10:19). Gaza was on the coast in the far southwest, so the raiders swept across the whole land from the Jordan to the sea.

decisions.choice: sustenance: food, what keeps people alive
decisions.reason: The word means the means of life. The raiders took or ruined the grain and drove off the animals, leaving people with nothing to live on (verse 6).

decisions.choice: the city of Gaza
decisions.reason: Readable says that Gaza was a city for readers who do not know the name.

records.source: כִּ֡י הֵם֩ וּמִקְנֵיהֶ֨ם יַעֲל֜וּ וְאָהֳלֵיהֶ֗ם וּבָ֤אוּ כְדֵֽי־אַרְבֶּה֙ לָרֹ֔ב וְלָהֶ֥ם וְלִגְמַלֵּיהֶ֖ם אֵ֣ין מִסְפָּ֑ר וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ בָאָ֖רֶץ לְשַׁחֲתָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: For they and their livestock would come up, and their tents, and they would come like [the] abundance of locust[s] for multitude; and to them and to their camels there was no number, and they came into the land to destroy it.
pieces: They came up with their livestock and their tents, as thick as a swarm of locusts. There was no counting them or their camels, and they came into the land to lay it waste.

L.5: For they and their livestock would come up, and their tents, and they would come like a swarm of locusts for multitude; and of them and of their camels there was no number; and they came into the land to destroy it.

R.5: They brought their animals and their tents with them. There were so many of them that they were like swarms of locusts. No one could count all the people and their camels. They came into the land to destroy it.

decisions.choice: they would come (the reading the scribes marked)
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "they would come" without "and"; the reading the scribes marked (qere) is "and they would come". Both use the same verb, and the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: like a swarm of locusts: countless and devouring everything
decisions.reason: Locusts are a picture both of vast numbers and of total ruin, as in the plague on Egypt, when they ate every green thing (Exodus 10:4-15). The raiders strip the land the same way.

decisions.choice: camels: the raiders rode camels
decisions.reason: Camels let desert peoples cover long distances quickly and carry off what they took. A force on camels in such numbers would have been terrifying to farmers on foot.

decisions.choice: to lay it waste
decisions.reason: Balanced varies the verb "destroy", used already in verse 4, with an expression that keeps its sense: to ruin the land completely.

records.source: וַיִּדַּ֧ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל מְאֹ֖ד מִפְּנֵ֣י מִדְיָ֑ן וַיִּזְעֲק֥וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל־יְהוָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And became low Israel very because of Midian, and cried out [the] sons of Israel to Yahweh.
pieces: Israel was reduced to great poverty because of Midian, and the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.6: And Israel was brought very low because of Midian, and the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.6: Israel became very poor because of the Midianites. So the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for help.

decisions.choice: was brought low: became poor and weak
decisions.reason: The verb means to become small, thin or poor. It is related to the word Gideon uses for his clan, "the weakest" (verse 15).

decisions.choice: cried out: called for help in distress
decisions.reason: The verb is used of people crying out under oppression, the step in the pattern of Judges that comes before Yahweh sends help (3:9, 15; 4:3).

decisions.choice: for help
decisions.reason: Readable adds "for help", as at each cry in the book (3:9, 15; 4:3; 10:10), to show what kind of crying out this was.

records.source: וַיְהִ֕י כִּֽי־זָעֲק֥וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל־יְהוָ֑ה עַ֖ל אֹד֥וֹת מִדְיָֽן׃
records.gloss: And it was, when cried out [the] sons of Israel to Yahweh on account of Midian,
pieces: When the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} because of Midian,

L.7: And it happened, when the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on account of Midian,

R.7: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for help because of what the Midianites were doing to them.

decisions.choice: the sentence runs on into verse 8
decisions.reason: "And it happened, when ..." sets the time for what follows: Yahweh's first answer is not a rescuer but a prophet with a rebuke (verses 8-10). Repeating the cry from verse 6 slows the story at this point.

decisions.choice: on account of Midian: because of what Midian was doing
decisions.reason: The phrase means "concerning" or "because of". Israel's cry is about Midian's raids, not yet about their own unfaithfulness, which the prophet will name.

decisions.choice: because of what the Midianites were doing to them
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what "on account of Midian" means, and ends the sentence here; verse 8 begins a new one with "So".

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֧ח יְהוָ֛ה אִ֥ישׁ נָבִ֖יא אֶל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לָהֶ֜ם כֹּה־אָמַ֥ר יְהוָ֣ה׀אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אָנֹכִ֞י הֶעֱלֵ֤יתִי אֶתְכֶם֙ מִמִּצְרַ֔יִם וָאֹצִ֥יא אֶתְכֶ֖ם מִבֵּ֥ית עֲבָדִֽים׃
records.gloss: and sent Yahweh a man, a prophet, to [the] sons of Israel, and he said to them, thus says Yahweh, God of Israel, I, I brought up you from Egypt and brought you out from [the] house of slaves.
pieces: {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent a prophet to the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}, and he said to them, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, says: 'It was I who brought you up from Egypt and led you out of the house of slavery.

L.8: and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent a man, a prophet, to the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel, and he said to them, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel: 'I, I brought you up from Egypt and brought you out from the house of slaves.

R.8: So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent a prophet to them. He said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, says this: 'I brought you up out of Egypt. I led you out of the land where you were slaves.

decisions.choice: a man, a prophet: a prophet whose name is not given
decisions.reason: The prophet is named only by his calling. Deborah too was a prophet (4:4). His message comes before any promise of rescue, so the people hear first why they are suffering.

decisions.choice: I, I brought you up: Yahweh and no other
decisions.reason: The pronoun "I" is stated in addition to the verb, which puts weight on it: it was Yahweh himself who rescued Israel, not the gods they now serve (verse 10).

decisions.choice: the house of slaves: Egypt, the place of slavery
decisions.reason: The words echo the opening of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2; Deuteronomy 5:6), which go on to forbid other gods. The prophet's message follows the same order: rescue first, then the claim to sole loyalty.

decisions.choice: slaves (Literal), slavery (Balanced), where you were slaves (Readable)
decisions.reason: This is Israel's slavery in Egypt, so every level keeps the word "slave", as the style guide asks for Exodus 20:2.

decisions.choice: double quotes for the prophet, single quotes for Yahweh's words
decisions.reason: The prophet speaks, and inside his speech he quotes Yahweh. Yahweh's words take single quotes; the words Yahweh says he once spoke to Israel (verse 10) take double quotes again.

records.source: וָאַצִּ֤ל אֶתְכֶם֙ מִיַּ֣ד מִצְרַ֔יִם וּמִיַּ֖ד כָּל־לֹחֲצֵיכֶ֑ם וָאֲגָרֵ֤שׁ אוֹתָם֙ מִפְּנֵיכֶ֔ם וָאֶתְּנָ֥ה לָכֶ֖ם אֶת־אַרְצָֽם׃
records.gloss: And I delivered you from [the] hand of Egypt and from [the] hand of all your oppressors, and I drove them out before you and gave to you their land.
pieces: I rescued you from the power of Egypt and from the power of everyone who oppressed you. I drove them out ahead of you and gave you their land.

L.9: And I delivered you from the hand of Egypt and from the hand of all your oppressors, and I drove them out before you and gave you their land.

R.9: I saved you from the Egyptians and from all the others who were cruel to you. I forced them out of the land as you came in, and I gave their land to you.

decisions.choice: from the hand of: from the power of
decisions.reason: As in verse 1, "hand" stands for power and control.

decisions.choice: your oppressors: those who pressed hard on you
decisions.reason: The verb means to press or squeeze. It is used of Egypt's oppression (Exodus 3:9) and of the enemies of the judges' time (2:18; 4:3).

decisions.choice: drove them out and gave you their land: the conquest under Joshua
decisions.reason: Yahweh recalls how he drove out the peoples of Canaan and gave Israel their land (Joshua 24:8-13), the same history Joshua told before the people chose to serve Yahweh alone.

decisions.choice: as you came in
decisions.reason: Readable explains "before you": the peoples were driven out as Israel entered the land.

records.source: וָאֹמְרָ֣ה לָכֶ֗ם אֲנִי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵיכֶ֔ם לֹ֤א תִֽירְאוּ֙ אֶת־אֱלֹהֵ֣י הָאֱמֹרִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַתֶּ֖ם יוֹשְׁבִ֣ים בְּאַרְצָ֑ם וְלֹ֥א שְׁמַעְתֶּ֖ם בְּקוֹלִֽי׃פ
records.gloss: And I said to you, I [am] Yahweh your God; not you shall fear [the] gods of the Amorite, whom you [are] dwelling in their land. But not you listened to my voice.
pieces: I said to you, "I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. You are not to fear the gods of the Amorites, though you live in their land." But you have not listened to me.'"

L.10: And I said to you, "I [am] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are dwelling." But you have not listened to my voice.'"

R.10: I said to you, "I am {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. Do not worship the gods of the Amorites, even though you live in their land." But you did not obey me.'"

decisions.choice: fear: revere and worship
decisions.reason: To "fear" a god is to stand in awe of it and serve it (2 Kings 17:35-38). Israel is not to give the gods of the land the worship that belongs to Yahweh.

decisions.choice: the Amorites: the peoples of Canaan in general
decisions.reason: "Amorite" is often used as a name for all the peoples who lived in the land before Israel (Genesis 15:16; Joshua 24:15).

decisions.choice: the message ends with the charge, with no promise
decisions.reason: The prophet stops at "you have not listened". There is no word of rescue; the answer to Israel's cry comes in the next scene, when the angel of Yahweh appears to Gideon (verse 11).

decisions.choice: Do not worship
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of "fear" here, to worship a god.

decisions.choice: listened to me (Balanced); obey me (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Listen to my voice" means to obey. Balanced drops "voice"; Readable says "obey".

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֞א מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֗ה וַיֵּ֨שֶׁב֙ תַּ֤חַת הָֽאֵלָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּעָפְרָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְיוֹאָ֖שׁ אֲבִ֣י הָֽעֶזְרִ֑י וְגִדְע֣וֹן בְּנ֗וֹ חֹבֵ֤ט חִטִּים֙ בַּגַּ֔ת לְהָנִ֖יס מִפְּנֵ֥י מִדְיָֽן׃
records.gloss: And came [the] angel of Yahweh and sat under the terebinth which [was] in Ophrah, which [belonged] to Joash the Abiezrite; and Gideon his son [was] beating out wheat in the winepress to hide [it] from before Midian.
pieces: Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Ophrah and sat down under the terebinth there, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite. Gideon, Joash's son, was beating out wheat in the winepress so that the Midianites would not see it.

L.11: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came and sat under the terebinth that [was] in Ophrah, which [belonged] to Joash the Abiezrite; and Gideon his son [was] beating out wheat in the winepress to hide [it] from Midian.

R.11: Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to the town of Ophrah. He sat down under a big tree there that belonged to Joash, from the family of Abiezer. Joash's son Gideon was beating the grain out of some wheat inside a winepress. He was doing it there so that the Midianites would not find the wheat.

decisions.choice: the angel of Yahweh: God's messenger, in whom God himself is present
decisions.reason: The word means "messenger". In this story the narrator calls the visitor "the angel of Yahweh" (verses 11, 12, 21, 22) and "the angel of God" (verse 20), but also says that "Yahweh turned to him" and "Yahweh said" (verses 14, 16, 23), and Gideon fears he will die because he has seen him face to face (verse 22). The same movement between the messenger and Yahweh himself is found in Genesis 16:7-13, Exodus 3:2-6 and 2:1-4 in this book. The text does not explain how the messenger and Yahweh are related.

decisions.choice: the terebinth: a large, long-lived tree
decisions.reason: The word names a big spreading tree, the terebinth or a kind of oak. Such trees were landmarks and were often places of worship, good or bad (Genesis 35:4; Joshua 24:26; 9:6 in this book).

decisions.choice: beating out wheat in the winepress: threshing in hiding
decisions.reason: Grain was normally threshed on an open threshing floor (verse 37), where the wind carried off the chaff. A winepress was a pit cut into the rock: hidden from view, but cramped. Beating the grain with a stick there, a little at a time, shows how afraid people were of the raiders.

decisions.choice: Joash the Abiezrite: a member of the clan of Abiezer in Manasseh
decisions.reason: Abiezer was a clan of the tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 17:2). Its town Ophrah is a different place from the Ophrah of Benjamin (Joshua 18:23), and its site is not known.

decisions.choice: a big tree; beating the grain out of some wheat
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for "terebinth" and for threshing, and adds why Gideon worked inside a winepress.

records.heading: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} calls Gideon

records.source: וַיֵּרָ֥א אֵלָ֖יו מַלְּאַ֣ךְיְהוָ֑ה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו יְהוָ֥ה עִמְּךָ֖ גִּבּ֥וֹר הֶחָֽיִל׃
records.gloss: And appeared to him [the] angel of Yahweh and said to him, Yahweh [is] with you, mighty [man] of strength.
pieces: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} appeared to him and said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is with you, mighty warrior."

L.12: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} appeared to him and said to him, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} [is] with you, mighty man of strength."

R.12: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} showed himself to Gideon and said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is with you, you strong fighter!"

decisions.choice: mighty man of strength: a strong warrior
decisions.reason: The phrase names a brave fighting man (11:1; Joshua 1:14). It can also mean a man of wealth and standing (Ruth 2:1; 1 Samuel 9:1). Spoken to a man hiding in a winepress, it sounds almost like irony, but it also says what Gideon will become with Yahweh's help.

decisions.choice: Yahweh is with you: a statement, not only a greeting
decisions.reason: The words can be a greeting (Ruth 2:4), but Gideon takes them as a claim and questions it (verse 13). Yahweh's promise in verse 16, "I will be with you", picks them up.

decisions.choice: appeared: let himself be seen
decisions.reason: The verb means "was seen". Gideon sees a visitor, but he does not yet know who he is (verse 22).

decisions.choice: showed himself to Gideon
decisions.reason: Readable puts the verb in active form and names Gideon for clarity.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֤יו גִּדְעוֹן֙ בִּ֣י אֲדֹנִ֔י וְיֵ֤שׁ יְהוָה֙ עִמָּ֔נוּ וְלָ֥מָּה מְצָאַ֖תְנוּ כָּל־זֹ֑את וְאַיֵּ֣ה כָֽל־נִפְלְאֹתָ֡יו אֲשֶׁר֩ סִפְּרוּ־לָ֨נוּ אֲבוֹתֵ֜ינוּ לֵאמֹ֗ר הֲלֹ֤א מִמִּצְרַ֨יִם֙ הֶעֱלָ֣נוּ יְהוָ֔ה וְעַתָּה֙ נְטָשָׁ֣נוּ יְהוָ֔ה וַֽיִּתְּנֵ֖נוּ בְּכַף־מִדְיָֽן׃
records.gloss: And said to him Gideon, pardon me, my lord, and if there is Yahweh with us, then why has found us all this? And where [are] all his wonders which recounted to us our fathers, saying, Did not from Egypt bring us up Yahweh? And now has abandoned us Yahweh and given us into [the] palm of Midian.
pieces: Gideon answered him, "Pardon me, my lord, but if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is with us, why has all this come upon us? Where are all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wonders that our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} told us about when they said, 'Did not {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} bring us up from Egypt?' Now {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has abandoned us and handed us over to Midian."

L.13: And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is with us, then why has all this found us? And where [are] all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wonders that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} bring us up from Egypt?' But now {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has abandoned us and given us into the palm of Midian."

R.13: Gideon said, "Excuse me, sir, but if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is with us, why has all this trouble come on us? Our {{gender:ancestors|fathers}} told us about the amazing things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did. They said, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} brought us up out of Egypt!' So where are those wonders now? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has left us and let the Midianites take control of us."

decisions.choice: please, my lord: a polite address to a stranger
decisions.reason: The vowels here mark the ordinary "my lord", the courteous way to speak to a superior, not the title used for God (contrast verse 15). Gideon treats the visitor as a man.

decisions.choice: with us: Gideon answers for all Israel
decisions.reason: The visitor said "with you", meaning Gideon alone (verse 12), but Gideon answers "with us". His complaint is about the whole people's suffering.

decisions.choice: wonders: the extraordinary acts of the exodus
decisions.reason: The word is used of the signs and deeds by which Yahweh brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:20; 34:10; Psalm 78:11-12).

decisions.choice: Yahweh has abandoned us: Gideon's complaint
decisions.reason: Gideon blames Yahweh for leaving Israel. The prophet has just given the other side: Israel did not listen to Yahweh (verse 10), and 2:12-14 says that Israel abandoned Yahweh first. Yahweh does not argue with Gideon but sends him (verse 14).

decisions.choice: 'The LORD brought us up out of Egypt!'
decisions.reason: The question "Did not the LORD bring us up?" expects the answer yes. Readable gives it as a statement, and moves Gideon's question "where are his wonders" after it.

decisions.choice: sir
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday polite word, since Gideon is speaking to someone he takes for a man.

records.source: וַיִּ֤פֶן אֵלָיו֙ יְהוָ֔ה וַיֹּ֗אמֶר לֵ֚ךְ בְּכֹחֲךָ֣ זֶ֔ה וְהוֹשַׁעְתָּ֥ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל מִכַּ֣ף מִדְיָ֑ן הֲלֹ֖א שְׁלַחְתִּֽיךָ׃
records.gloss: And turned to him Yahweh and said, Go in this your strength, and you will deliver Israel from [the] palm of Midian. Have not I sent you?
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} turned to him and said, "Go in this strength of yours, and you will save Israel from Midian's power. Am I not the one sending you?"

L.14: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} turned to him and said, "Go in this strength of yours, and you will deliver Israel from the palm of Midian. Have I not sent you?"

R.14: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} turned toward him and said, "Go with the strength you have, and rescue Israel from the Midianites. I am the one who is sending you!"

decisions.choice: Yahweh turned to him: the visitor now speaks as Yahweh
decisions.reason: The narrator no longer says "the angel of Yahweh" but "Yahweh", and the visitor speaks with Yahweh's own authority: "Have I not sent you?" See verse 11.

decisions.choice: this strength of yours: the strength you have now
alternatives: the strength I have just spoken of
decisions.reason: "This" may point to Gideon's strength as it is, weak as he thinks it (verse 15), or to the strength promised in verse 12, "Yahweh is with you". Either way Gideon is to go as he is, without waiting to become stronger.

decisions.choice: deliver: rescue from an enemy
decisions.reason: This is the work of the judges whom Yahweh raised up (2:16, 18; 3:9, 31).

decisions.choice: Have I not sent you?: a firm statement
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer yes. It is Yahweh's commission, like the sending of Moses (Exodus 3:10-12).

decisions.choice: pronouns for the visitor follow the narrator's name for him
decisions.reason: Where the narrator calls the speaker "the LORD" (verses 14-18, 23), English marks the pronouns for him as pronouns for God; where he is called "the angel", it does not.

decisions.choice: I am the one who is sending you!
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the statement it implies.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ בִּ֣י אֲדֹנָ֔י בַּמָּ֥ה אוֹשִׁ֖יעַ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל הִנֵּ֤ה אַלְפִּי֙ הַדַּ֣ל בִּמְנַשֶּׁ֔ה וְאָנֹכִ֥י הַצָּעִ֖יר בְּבֵ֥ית אָבִֽי׃
records.gloss: And he said to him, pardon me, my Lord, by what will I deliver Israel? Look, my clan [is] the weak[est] in Manasseh, and I [am] the least in [the] house of my father.
pieces: Gideon said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Pardon me, my Lord, but how can I save Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my family."

L.15: And he said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Please, my Lord, how will I deliver Israel? Look, my clan [is] the weakest in Manasseh, and I [am] the least in my father's house."

R.15: Gideon said, "Please, Lord, how could I rescue Israel? My clan is the weakest one in the tribe of Manasseh. And in my family I am the least important."

decisions.choice: my Lord: the vowels mark the title used for God
decisions.reason: The consonants are the same as "my lord" in verse 13, but here the scribes pointed the word as the title reserved for God. They read Gideon as now speaking to Yahweh, who has just spoken to him (verse 14). Gideon himself may still be speaking politely to a stranger, since he only realizes who the visitor is in verse 22.

decisions.choice: my clan: the word often means "thousand"
decisions.reason: The word usually means "a thousand", but it can name a clan or a fighting unit raised from a clan (1 Samuel 10:19; see Numbers 1). Here it is Gideon's clan, Abiezer.

decisions.choice: the least: the youngest or the smallest in standing
decisions.reason: The word can mean "youngest" or "most insignificant". Either way Gideon says he is the last person anyone would choose. Yahweh often chooses the least likely (1 Samuel 9:21; 16:11).

decisions.choice: my family
decisions.reason: "My father's house" means the extended family Gideon belongs to.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֥י אֶהְיֶ֖ה עִמָּ֑ךְ וְהִכִּיתָ֥ אֶת־מִדְיָ֖ן כְּאִ֥ישׁ אֶחָֽד׃
records.gloss: And said to him Yahweh, surely I will be with you, and you will strike Midian as one man.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} answered him, "I will be with you, and you will strike down the Midianites as if they were one man."

L.16: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Surely I will be with you, and you will strike down Midian as one man."

R.16: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "I will be with you. You will defeat all the Midianites as easily as if you were fighting just one man."

decisions.choice: I will be with you: the promise made to Moses
decisions.reason: Yahweh used the same words when he sent Moses to Pharaoh and Moses protested that he was unfit (Exodus 3:11-12). Gideon's weakness is answered with Yahweh's presence, not with a reason to trust himself.

decisions.choice: as one man: all at once, as easily as one man
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean that the enemy will fall together, in one blow (Numbers 14:15), or that defeating them will be as easy as defeating a single man. Both point to a complete victory.

decisions.choice: as easily as if you were fighting just one man
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture; see m2.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו אִם־נָ֛א מָצָ֥אתִי חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֶ֑יךָ וְעָשִׂ֤יתָ לִּי֙ א֔וֹת שָׁאַתָּ֖ה מְדַבֵּ֥ר עִמִּֽי׃
records.gloss: And he said to him, if please I have found favor in your eyes, then make for me a sign that you [are] speaking with me.
pieces: Gideon said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "If I have found favor with {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, give me a sign that it is really {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} who are speaking to me.

L.17: And he said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "If now I have found favor in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} eyes, then make for me a sign that [it is] {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} speaking with me.

R.17: Gideon said, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are pleased with me, please show me a sign. Then I will know that it is really {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} talking to me.

decisions.choice: if I have found favor in your eyes: a polite request
decisions.reason: The phrase is a courteous way to ask a favor of someone greater (Genesis 18:3; Exodus 33:13).

decisions.choice: sign: proof
decisions.reason: Gideon asks for something that will show the promise is real, as Moses was given signs (Exodus 3:12; 4:1-9). The sign comes in verse 21.

decisions.choice: that you are speaking with me: that it is really you
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is stressed. Gideon wants to know who is speaking: whether this visitor truly speaks for Yahweh.

decisions.choice: the quotation runs on into verse 18
decisions.reason: Gideon's words continue in the next verse, so the closing quotation mark comes there.

records.source: אַל־נָ֨א תָמֻ֤שׁ מִזֶּה֙ עַד־בֹּאִ֣י אֵלֶ֔יךָ וְהֹֽצֵאתִי֙ אֶת־מִנְחָתִ֔י וְהִנַּחְתִּ֖י לְפָנֶ֑יךָ וַיֹּאמַ֕ר אָנֹכִ֥י אֵשֵׁ֖ב עַ֥ד שׁוּבֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: Do not, please, depart from here until my coming to you and I bring out my gift and set [it] before you. And he said, I, I will stay until your return.
pieces: Please do not leave here until I come back to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} and bring out my offering and set it before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}." He said, "I will stay until you come back."

L.18: Please do not depart from here until I come to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} and bring out my offering and set [it] before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}." And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "I, I will stay until you return."

R.18: Please do not leave until I come back with a gift of food for {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}." He answered, "I will wait here until you come back."

decisions.choice: my offering: a gift, which could be a meal or a sacrifice
decisions.reason: The word means a gift brought to honor someone, and it is also the word for the grain offering in worship (Leviticus 2:1). Gideon may be preparing a meal for an honored guest, as Abraham did (Genesis 18:1-8), or an offering; the visitor turns it into an offering by fire (verse 21).

decisions.choice: I, I will stay: I myself will wait
decisions.reason: The pronoun "I" is stressed: the visitor himself promises to wait for Gideon.

decisions.choice: a gift of food
decisions.reason: Readable says what the gift turns out to be (verse 19).

decisions.choice: come back
decisions.reason: Gideon will leave and "come" to the visitor again; Balanced and Readable say "come back".

records.source: וְגִדְע֣וֹן בָּ֗א וַיַּ֤עַשׂ גְּדִֽי־עִזִּים֙ וְאֵיפַת־קֶ֣מַח מַצּ֔וֹת הַבָּשָׂר֙ שָׂ֣ם בַּסַּ֔ל וְהַמָּרַ֖ק שָׂ֣ם בַּפָּר֑וּר וַיּוֹצֵ֥א אֵלָ֛יו אֶל־תַּ֥חַת הָאֵלָ֖ה וַיַּגַּֽשׁ׃ס
records.gloss: And Gideon went and prepared a kid of goats and an ephah of flour [as] unleavened [bread]; the meat he put in the basket, and the broth he put in the pot, and he brought [them] out to him to under the terebinth and presented [them].
pieces: Gideon went in and prepared a young goat, and unleavened bread from {{units:about 20 quarts|an ephah}} of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, brought them out to him under the terebinth, and set them before him.

L.19: And Gideon went in and prepared a young goat, and unleavened [bread from] an ephah of flour. The meat he put in the basket, and the broth he put in the pot, and he brought [them] out to him under the terebinth and presented [them].

R.19: Gideon went and cooked a young goat. He also used {{units:about 20 quarts|an ephah}} of flour to bake bread without yeast. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot. Then he brought the food out to the angel under the tree and offered it to him.

decisions.choice: an ephah of flour: a very large amount
decisions.reason: An ephah was a dry measure of about 20 quarts (roughly 22 liters), far more bread than one guest could eat. It was a generous gift, all the more so in a time when the raiders left little food (verses 4-6).

decisions.choice: unleavened bread: bread made quickly, without yeast
decisions.reason: Bread without yeast could be baked at once, without waiting for the dough to rise, as when Lot fed his guests (Genesis 19:3).

decisions.choice: presented: brought near, as a gift or an offering
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring something close. It is also used of bringing offerings to God (Amos 5:25; Malachi 1:7).

decisions.choice: {{units:about 20 quarts|an ephah}}
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern measure, with the ephah as the alternative.

decisions.choice: the angel
decisions.reason: Readable names the one Gideon brought the food to.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֜יו מַלְאַ֣ךְ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים קַ֣ח אֶת־הַבָּשָׂ֤ר וְאֶת־הַמַּצּוֹת֙ וְהַנַּח֙ אֶל־הַסֶּ֣לַע הַלָּ֔ז וְאֶת־הַמָּרַ֖ק שְׁפ֑וֹךְ וַיַּ֖עַשׂ כֵּֽן׃
records.gloss: And said to him [the] angel of God, take the meat and the unleavened [bread] and set [them] on this rock, and the broth pour out. And he did so.
pieces: The angel of God told him, "Take the meat and the unleavened bread, and place them on this rock. Then pour the broth out." And he did so.

L.20: And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened [bread] and set [them] on this rock, and pour out the broth." And he did so.

R.20: The angel of God told him, "Take the meat and the bread and put them on this rock. Then pour out the broth." Gideon did what he said.

decisions.choice: the angel of God: the same visitor
decisions.reason: The narrator now says "the angel of God" for the one he calls "the angel of Yahweh" in verses 11 and 21; the two names are used of the same figure in 13:3, 6, 9.

decisions.choice: this rock: a natural altar
decisions.reason: The rock takes the place of an altar, and pouring out the broth is like pouring out a drink offering. The meal is being turned into a sacrifice, as in 13:19.

decisions.choice: the bread
decisions.reason: Readable has already said that the bread was made without yeast (verse 19), so it does not repeat it.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֞ח מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֗ה אֶת־קְצֵ֤ה הַמִּשְׁעֶ֨נֶת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּיָד֔וֹ וַיִּגַּ֥ע בַּבָּשָׂ֖ר וּבַמַּצּ֑וֹת וַתַּ֨עַל הָאֵ֜שׁ מִן־הַצּ֗וּר וַתֹּ֤אכַל אֶת־הַבָּשָׂר֙ וְאֶת־הַמַּצּ֔וֹת וּמַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה הָלַ֖ךְ מֵעֵינָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And stretched out [the] angel of Yahweh [the] tip of the staff which [was] in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened [bread], and went up the fire from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened [bread]; and [the] angel of Yahweh went from his eyes.
pieces: Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} reached out the tip of the staff in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. Fire flared up from the rock and burned up the meat and the bread, and the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} vanished from his sight.

L.21: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} stretched out the tip of the staff that [was] in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened [bread]; and the fire went up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened [bread]. And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} went from his eyes.

R.21: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} reached out with the staff he was holding and touched the meat and the bread with the tip of it. Fire blazed up out of the rock and burned up all the food. Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} disappeared.

decisions.choice: fire from the rock: the sign Gideon asked for
decisions.reason: This is the sign of verse 17. Fire that consumes an offering shows that God accepts it (Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38), and a visitor who can do this is no ordinary man.

decisions.choice: went from his eyes: disappeared from his sight
decisions.reason: The visitor does not walk away; he is suddenly gone, as the angel goes up in the flame in 13:20.

decisions.choice: all the food
decisions.reason: Readable sums up "the meat and the unleavened bread" in one phrase.

records.source: וַיַּ֣רְא גִּדְע֔וֹן כִּֽי־מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָ֖ה ה֑וּאסוַיֹּ֣אמֶר גִּדְע֗וֹן אֲהָהּ֙ אֲדֹנָ֣י יְהוִ֔ה כִּֽי־עַל־כֵּ֤ן רָאִ֨יתִי֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה פָּנִ֖ים אֶל־פָּנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And saw Gideon that [the] angel of Yahweh [was] he, and said Gideon, alas, Lord Yahweh! For because of this I have seen [the] angel of Yahweh face to face.
pieces: When Gideon saw that it was the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, he cried out, "How terrible, {{divine_name:Lord GOD|Lord Yahweh}}! I have looked on the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} face to face!"

L.22: And Gideon saw that he [was] the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and Gideon said, "Alas, {{divine_name:Lord GOD|Lord Yahweh}}! For indeed I have seen the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} face to face."

R.22: Then Gideon understood that it had been the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. He cried out, "Oh no, {{divine_name:Lord GOD|Lord Yahweh}}! I saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} face to face!"

decisions.choice: face to face: Gideon fears he will die
decisions.reason: It was believed that no one could see God and live (Exodus 33:20; Genesis 32:31; 13:22 in this book). By crying out, Gideon shows he now knows that in the angel he has met Yahweh himself. Yahweh's answer comes in verse 23.

decisions.choice: alas: a cry of alarm
decisions.reason: The word is a cry of dismay, used when someone fears disaster (Joshua 7:7; Jeremiah 1:6).

decisions.choice: for indeed: the reason for his alarm
decisions.reason: The words introduce what has happened that makes Gideon cry out. They can be read "for this is why" or "because"; the point is the same: he has seen the angel of Yahweh.

decisions.choice: Lord GOD
decisions.reason: Where "Lord" stands before the divine name, the name is printed "GOD" to avoid "Lord LORD", as elsewhere in the translation.

decisions.choice: How terrible (Balanced); Oh no (Readable)
decisions.reason: Modern English for the cry of dismay; "alas" sounds old-fashioned.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר ל֧וֹ יְהוָ֛ה שָׁל֥וֹם לְךָ֖ אַל־תִּירָ֑א לֹ֖א תָּמֽוּת׃
records.gloss: And said to him Yahweh, peace to you; do not fear, not you will die.
pieces: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Peace to you! Do not be afraid; you will not die."

L.23: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Peace to you; do not fear; you will not die."

R.23: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told him, "Peace be with you. Do not be afraid. You will not die."

decisions.choice: peace: safety and well-being
decisions.reason: The word is a greeting, but here it is also an assurance: Gideon is safe and no harm will come to him. Gideon names the altar after this word (verse 24).

decisions.choice: Yahweh speaks after the angel is gone
decisions.reason: The angel has vanished (verse 21), but Yahweh still speaks to Gideon. The text does not say how; perhaps as a voice, as in the night in verse 25.

decisions.choice: But
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that Yahweh's words answer Gideon's fear.

records.source: וַיִּבֶן֩ שָׁ֨ם גִּדְע֤וֹן מִזְבֵּ֨חַ֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה וַיִּקְרָא־ל֥וֹ יְהוָ֖ה שָׁל֑וֹם עַ֚ד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה עוֹדֶ֕נּוּ בְּעָפְרָ֖ת אֲבִ֥י הָעֶזְרִֽי׃פ
records.gloss: And built there Gideon an altar to Yahweh and called it Yahweh [is] peace. Until this day it [is] still in Ophrah of [the] Abiezrite.
pieces: So Gideon built an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} there and named it "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} Is Peace." To this day it still stands in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

L.24: And Gideon built an altar there to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and called it "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} [Is] Peace." To this day it [is] still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

R.24: Gideon built an altar there to worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. He named it "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} Is Peace." It is still there today in Ophrah, the town of Abiezer's family.

decisions.choice: Yahweh is peace: the altar remembers Yahweh's word to Gideon
decisions.reason: The name repeats Yahweh's assurance in verse 23, "Peace to you". Gideon has seen Yahweh's messenger and lived. Other altars were named in the same way after what God had done (Genesis 22:14; Exodus 17:15).

decisions.choice: to this day: the writer's own time
decisions.reason: The altar was still known in Ophrah when the book was written.

decisions.choice: to worship; the town of Abiezer's family
decisions.reason: Readable says what an altar was for and explains "Ophrah of the Abiezrites".

records.source: וַיְהִי֮ בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַהוּא֒ וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ יְהוָ֗ה קַ֤ח אֶת־פַּר־הַשּׁוֹר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְאָבִ֔יךָ וּפַ֥ר הַשֵּׁנִ֖י שֶׁ֣בַע שָׁנִ֑ים וְהָרַסְתָּ֗ אֶת־מִזְבַּ֤ח הַבַּ֨עַל֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְאָבִ֔יךָ וְאֶת־הָאֲשֵׁרָ֥ה אֲשֶׁר־עָלָ֖יו תִּכְרֹֽת׃
records.gloss: And it was in that night, and said to him Yahweh, take [the] bull of the ox[en] which [belongs] to your father, and [the] second bull, seven years [old], and tear down [the] altar of the Baal which [belongs] to your father, and the Asherah which [is] beside it cut down.
pieces: That same night {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Take the young bull from your father's herd, the second bull, the one seven years old. Tear down the altar of Baal that belongs to your father, and cut down the Asherah pole next to it.

L.25: And it happened that night that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Take the young bull of the cattle that belongs to your father, and the second bull, seven years [old], and tear down the altar of the Baal that belongs to your father, and cut down the Asherah pole that [is] beside it.

R.25: That night {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Gideon, "Take one of your father's bulls, the second one, which is seven years old. Pull down your father's altar to the god Baal. Cut down the pole beside it that is used to worship the goddess Asherah.

decisions.choice: the bull ... the second bull: probably one bull, described twice
alternatives: two bulls: your father's bull and a second bull
decisions.reason: The Hebrew can be read as two animals, "your father's bull and the second bull", or as one, "your father's bull, that is, the second bull". Only "the second bull" is offered (verses 26, 28), so one bull is the more likely reading. "Second" may mean second in age or rank, or the next best after the first.

decisions.choice: the altar of Baal that belongs to your father: a family shrine to Baal
decisions.reason: Baal was the Canaanite storm god, believed to send rain and harvests. The altar belonged to Gideon's own father, which shows how far the worship the prophet condemned (verse 10) had reached into Israel's families (2:11-13).

decisions.choice: the Asherah: a wooden pole for the goddess Asherah
decisions.reason: Asherah was a Canaanite goddess, and her symbol, a wooden pole or tree, stood beside an altar. Israel had been told to cut such poles down (Exodus 34:13; Deuteronomy 7:5).

decisions.choice: seven years old: as many years as Midian's rule
decisions.reason: The bull's age matches the seven years of oppression (verse 1), so its sacrifice may mark the end of that time.

decisions.choice: the god Baal; the pole ... used to worship the goddess Asherah
decisions.reason: Readable says who Baal and Asherah were and what the pole was for. After this it calls it "the Asherah pole".

records.heading: Gideon tears down Baal's altar

records.source: וּבָנִ֨יתָ מִזְבֵּ֜חַ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ עַ֣ל רֹ֧אשׁ הַמָּע֛וֹז הַזֶּ֖ה בַּמַּֽעֲרָכָ֑ה וְלָֽקַחְתָּ֙ אֶת־הַפָּ֣ר הַשֵּׁנִ֔י וְהַעֲלִ֣יתָ עוֹלָ֔ה בַּעֲצֵ֥י הָאֲשֵׁרָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּכְרֹֽת׃
records.gloss: And build an altar to Yahweh your God on [the] top of this stronghold in the arrangement, and take the second bull and offer up a burnt offering with [the] wood of the Asherah which you will cut down.
pieces: Then build an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God on top of this stronghold, laid out in the proper way. Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering, using the wood of the Asherah pole that you cut down."

L.26: And build an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God on [the] top of this stronghold, in the [proper] arrangement, and take the second bull and offer [it as] a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah pole that you will cut down."

R.26: Then build an altar to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God on top of this high, safe place, and build it the right way. Take the second bull and offer it on the altar as a burnt offering. Use the wood of the Asherah pole that you cut down for the fire."

decisions.choice: this stronghold: a high place of safety
decisions.reason: The word means a place of refuge or a fortress. It may be the fortified height of the town, or a rocky place near it like the strongholds of verse 2.

decisions.choice: in the proper arrangement: built and laid out in the right way
alternatives: with the wood laid in order
decisions.reason: The word means an ordered row or arrangement. It may refer to the stones of the altar set in order, or to the wood laid out on it, as the priests arranged wood on the altar (Leviticus 1:7-8). Either way the new altar is to be properly made.

decisions.choice: the wood of the Asherah: the goddess's symbol burns in Yahweh's offering
decisions.reason: The pole that stood for the goddess becomes firewood for a sacrifice to Yahweh, a public sign that she has no power.

decisions.choice: high, safe place
decisions.reason: Readable explains "stronghold".

records.source: וַיִּקַּ֨ח גִּדְע֜וֹן עֲשָׂרָ֤ה אֲנָשִׁים֙ מֵֽעֲבָדָ֔יו וַיַּ֕עַשׂ כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר דִּבֶּ֥ר אֵלָ֖יו יְהוָ֑ה וַיְהִ֡י כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר יָרֵא֩ אֶת־בֵּ֨ית אָבִ֜יו וְאֶת־אַנְשֵׁ֥י הָעִ֛יר מֵעֲשׂ֥וֹת יוֹמָ֖ם וַיַּ֥עַשׂ לָֽיְלָה׃
records.gloss: And took Gideon ten men from his slaves and did just as had spoken to him Yahweh; and it was, because he feared [the] house of his father and [the] men of the city to do [it] by day, and he did [it at] night.
pieces: So Gideon took ten men from among his servants and did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had told him. But he was too afraid of his father's family and the men of the town to do it by day, so he did it at night.

L.27: And Gideon took ten men from his slaves and did as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had spoken to him. But because he feared his father's house and the men of the city too much to do [it] by day, he did [it at] night.

R.27: So Gideon took ten of his servants and did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told him. But he was afraid of his family and of the men in the town. So he did it at night instead of during the day.

decisions.choice: ten men from his slaves: men who belonged to the household
decisions.reason: The word names men owned by the household, not hired workers. That Gideon had ten such men to call on suggests a family of some standing, though he called himself the least (verse 15).

decisions.choice: afraid to do it by day, so he did it at night
decisions.reason: Gideon obeys fully, but his fear decides the time. The text records both without comment.

decisions.choice: the men of the city: the townsmen
decisions.reason: These are the men of Ophrah, probably the heads of families who answered for the town's affairs; they demand Gideon's death in verse 30.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: As the style guide asks, Balanced and Readable say "servants" and Literal "slaves"; the meaning decision m1 keeps the hard sense of the word.

records.source: וַיַּשְׁכִּ֜ימוּ אַנְשֵׁ֤י הָעִיר֙ בַּבֹּ֔קֶר וְהִנֵּ֤ה נֻתַּץ֙ מִזְבַּ֣ח הַבַּ֔עַל וְהָאֲשֵׁרָ֥ה אֲשֶׁר־עָלָ֖יו כֹּרָ֑תָה וְאֵת֙ הַפָּ֣ר הַשֵּׁנִ֔י הֹֽעֲלָ֔ה עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּ֖חַ הַבָּנֽוּי׃
records.gloss: And rose early [the] men of the city in the morning, and look, had been torn down [the] altar of the Baal, and the Asherah which [was] beside it had been cut down, and the second bull had been offered up on the altar [that had been] built.
pieces: When the men of the town got up early in the morning, they saw that Baal's altar had been torn down and the Asherah pole beside it cut down, and that the second bull had been offered on the altar that had been built.

L.28: And the men of the city rose early in the morning, and look, the altar of the Baal had been torn down, and the Asherah pole that [was] beside it had been cut down, and the second bull had been offered on the altar [that had been] built.

R.28: Early the next morning the men of the town got up. They saw that the altar of Baal had been pulled down and the Asherah pole beside it had been cut down. And they saw that the second bull had been offered as a sacrifice on the new altar.

decisions.choice: look: the scene as the townsmen saw it
decisions.reason: The word draws the reader into what the men saw when they came out in the morning.

decisions.choice: had been torn down, cut down, offered: no one is named
decisions.reason: All three verbs are passive. The men see what has been done but not who did it, which leads to their question in verse 29.

decisions.choice: they saw that
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "look" stands for.

records.source: וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֔הוּ מִ֥י עָשָׂ֖ה הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַֽיִּדְרְשׁוּ֙ וַיְבַקְשׁ֔וּ וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ גִּדְעוֹן֙ בֶּן־יוֹאָ֔שׁ עָשָׂ֖ה הַדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And they said each to his neighbor, who has done this thing? And they inquired and searched, and they said, Gideon son of Joash has done this thing.
pieces: They asked one another, "Who has done this?" After they had asked around and looked into it, they said, "Gideon son of Joash did it."

L.29: And they said each to his neighbor, "Who has done this thing?" And they inquired and searched, and they said, "Gideon son of Joash has done this thing."

R.29: They asked each other, "Who did this?" They asked questions and searched for the answer. Then they said, "Gideon, the son of Joash, did it."

decisions.choice: each to his neighbor: to one another
decisions.reason: The phrase means that they asked each other.

decisions.choice: inquired and searched: a careful investigation
decisions.reason: The same verbs are used in Deuteronomy 13:15 and 17:4 for looking into a report that someone has served other gods. Here the town investigates the man who destroyed Baal's altar.

decisions.choice: this; it
decisions.reason: "This thing" is shortened to "this" and "it", the natural English.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמְר֜וּ אַנְשֵׁ֤י הָעִיר֙ אֶל־יוֹאָ֔שׁ הוֹצֵ֥א אֶת־בִּנְךָ֖ וְיָמֹ֑ת כִּ֤י נָתַץ֙ אֶת־מִזְבַּ֣ח הַבַּ֔עַל וְכִ֥י כָרַ֖ת הָאֲשֵׁרָ֥ה אֲשֶׁר־עָלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And said [the] men of the city to Joash, bring out your son that he may die, for he has torn down [the] altar of the Baal, and for he has cut down the Asherah which [was] beside it.
pieces: The men of the town said to Joash, "Bring your son out. He must die, for he has torn down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah pole that stood beside it."

L.30: And the men of the city said to Joash, "Bring out your son, and let him die, for he has torn down the altar of the Baal, and he has cut down the Asherah pole that [was] beside it."

R.30: The men of the town said to Joash, "Bring your son out here. He must be killed! He pulled down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah pole that was next to it."

decisions.choice: bring out your son, that he may die: a reversal of the law
decisions.reason: The law said that anyone who led Israel to serve other gods must be put to death, even a close relative (Deuteronomy 13:7-11; 17:2-5). Here the town demands death for the man who destroyed a false god's altar.

decisions.choice: for ... and for: two charges
decisions.reason: The townsmen list two crimes: tearing down the altar and cutting down the pole.

decisions.choice: He must be killed!
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that the men want Gideon put to death.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֡שׁ לְכֹל֩ אֲשֶׁר־עָמְד֨וּ עָלָ֜יו הַאַתֶּ֣ם׀תְּרִיב֣וּן לַבַּ֗עַל אִם־אַתֶּם֙ תּוֹשִׁיע֣וּן אוֹת֔וֹ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָרִ֥יב ל֛וֹ יוּמַ֖ת עַד־הַבֹּ֑קֶר אִם־אֱלֹהִ֥ים הוּא֙ יָ֣רֶב ל֔וֹ כִּ֥י נָתַ֖ץ אֶֽת־מִזְבְּחֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And said Joash to all who stood against him, will you contend for the Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him will be put to death by the morning. If [he is] a god, let him contend for himself, for he has torn down his altar.
pieces: But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Are you going to plead Baal's case? Are you going to rescue him? By morning, anyone who pleads his case will be put to death! If Baal is a god, he should plead his own case, since it is his altar that has been torn down."

L.31: And Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for the Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he [is] a god, let him contend for himself, because he has torn down his altar."

R.31: But Joash answered the crowd that stood against him, "Are you going to argue for Baal? Do you think you have to rescue him? Anyone who argues for Baal will be put to death by morning! If Baal really is a god, he can argue for himself. It was his altar that was pulled down."

decisions.choice: contend: plead a case, argue or fight for someone
decisions.reason: The verb is used of taking someone's side in a dispute, in court or by force. Joash says three times that a real god would take up his own case. The same verb gives Gideon his new name (verse 32).

decisions.choice: if he is a god: a god who cannot defend himself is no god
decisions.reason: Joash turns the charge around: if Baal needs men to protect him, he is not worth protecting. Elijah mocks Baal in the same way (1 Kings 18:27).

decisions.choice: he has torn down his altar: Gideon tore down Baal's altar
decisions.reason: "He" is Gideon and "his altar" is Baal's. Joash does not deny what his son did; he leaves Baal to answer it.

decisions.choice: by morning: at once, before another day passes
decisions.reason: It is already morning (verse 28), so the words may mean "while it is still morning" or "before tomorrow morning". Either way Joash threatens a swift penalty on anyone who defends Baal.

decisions.choice: plead his case (Balanced); argue for (Readable)
decisions.reason: English has no one word for "contend" that keeps both the legal and the fighting sense. Balanced uses the language of a court case, which suits Joash's challenge; Readable says "argue".

decisions.choice: If Baal is a god (Balanced); Anyone who argues for Baal; If Baal really is a god (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Baal where the Hebrew says "he" or "him", so the reader does not take the pronoun for Gideon.

records.source: וַיִּקְרָא־ל֥וֹ בַיּוֹם־הַה֖וּא יְרֻבַּ֣עַל לֵאמֹ֑ר יָ֤רֶב בּוֹ֙ הַבַּ֔עַל כִּ֥י נָתַ֖ץ אֶֽת־מִזְבְּחֽוֹ׃פ
records.gloss: And he called him on that day Jerubbaal, saying, let contend against him the Baal, for he has torn down his altar.
pieces: So on that day Gideon was given the name Jerubbaal, for it was said, "Let Baal contend against him, because he tore down his altar."

L.32: And on that day he called him Jerubbaal, saying, "Let the Baal contend against him, because he has torn down his altar."

R.32: From that day on, Gideon was also called Jerubbaal. The name means "Let Baal argue against him." He was given this name because he had pulled down Baal's altar.

decisions.choice: Jerubbaal: "let Baal contend"
decisions.reason: The name sounds like the words "let Baal contend", taken from Joash's challenge (verse 31). Names of this form can also mean "Baal contends" or "Baal is great", but the story reads it as a dare that Baal never takes up. Gideon is called Jerubbaal again in 7:1 and 8:29-35, and in 2 Samuel 11:21 he is called Jerubbesheth, with the word "shame" in place of Baal.

decisions.choice: he called him: probably Joash, or people in general
decisions.reason: The verb has "he" as its subject. It is most naturally Joash, who has just spoken, but the form can also mean simply that Gideon was called this.

decisions.choice: was given the name (Balanced); was also called (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable do not name who gave the name; see m2. Readable adds "also" because the book goes on to use both names (7:1).

decisions.choice: The name means
decisions.reason: Readable explains the wordplay the Hebrew reader would hear at once.

records.source: וְכָל־מִדְיָ֧ן וַעֲמָלֵ֛ק וּבְנֵי־קֶ֖דֶם נֶאֶסְפ֣וּ יַחְדָּ֑ו וַיַּעַבְר֥וּ וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ בְּעֵ֥מֶק יִזְרְעֶֽאל׃
records.gloss: And all Midian and Amalek and [the] sons of [the] east gathered together and crossed over and camped in [the] valley of Jezreel.
pieces: Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the peoples of the east joined forces, crossed the Jordan, and camped in the Valley of Jezreel.

L.33: And all Midian and Amalek and the {{gender:people|sons}} of the east gathered together, and they crossed over and camped in the valley of Jezreel.

R.33: Then all the Midianites, the Amalekites and the other people from the east came together. They crossed the Jordan River and set up camp in the Jezreel Valley.

decisions.choice: crossed over: crossed the Jordan from the east
decisions.reason: The raiders came from the desert east of the Jordan (verse 3), so "crossed over" means crossing the river into the land.

decisions.choice: the valley of Jezreel: the broad plain in the north
decisions.reason: The valley ran east and west between the hills of Galilee and those of Manasseh. It was rich farmland and an open road for raiders on camels (Joshua 17:16).

decisions.choice: the Jordan
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the river, which the Hebrew leaves understood.

records.heading: Gideon calls out the tribes

records.source: וְר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֔ה לָבְשָׁ֖ה אֶת־גִּדְע֑וֹן וַיִּתְקַע֙ בַּשּׁוֹפָ֔ר וַיִזָּעֵ֥קאֲבִיעֶ֖זֶר אַחֲרָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And [the] Spirit of Yahweh clothed Gideon, and he blew on the horn, and was called out Abiezer after him.
pieces: Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} clothed Gideon. He blew the ram's horn, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.

L.34: And the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} clothed Gideon, and he blew the trumpet, and Abiezer was summoned after him.

R.34: Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came on Gideon and took hold of him. He blew a trumpet to call the men of his clan, the family of Abiezer, to follow him.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of Yahweh clothed Gideon: took him over completely
decisions.reason: The verb means to put on clothes. The Spirit wraps Gideon like a garment and acts through him (1 Chronicles 12:19; 2 Chronicles 24:20). Elsewhere in Judges the Spirit "came on" the judges (3:10; 11:29); this picture is stronger.

decisions.choice: the trumpet: a ram's horn blown to call men to war
decisions.reason: The shofar, a ram's horn, gave the signal for battle (3:27).

decisions.choice: Abiezer was summoned: Gideon's clan came out
decisions.reason: "Abiezer" is the clan as a whole. The same form of the verb is used in verse 35 for Manasseh.

decisions.choice: came on Gideon and took hold of him
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of clothing: the Spirit came on Gideon and took control.

decisions.choice: trumpet (L, R); ram's horn (B)
decisions.reason: As in Joshua 6 and Judges 7: Literal and Readable use the familiar word "trumpet", and Balanced names the instrument.

records.source: וּמַלְאָכִים֙ שָׁלַ֣ח בְּכָל־מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה וַיִזָּעֵ֥קגַּם־ה֖וּא אַחֲרָ֑יו וּמַלְאָכִ֣ים שָׁלַ֗ח בְּאָשֵׁ֤ר וּבִזְבֻלוּן֙ וּבְנַפְתָּלִ֔י וַֽיַּעֲל֖וּ לִקְרָאתָֽם׃
records.gloss: And messengers he sent throughout all Manasseh, and was called out also it after him; and messengers he sent in Asher and in Zebulun and in Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.
pieces: He sent messengers all through Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. He also sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, and they came up to join them.

L.35: And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and it too was summoned after him; and he sent messengers to Asher and to Zebulun and to Naphtali, and they came up to meet them.

R.35: He sent messengers all through the tribe of Manasseh to call its men to follow him, and they came. He also sent messengers to the tribes of Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali. Their men came up to join Gideon and his men.

decisions.choice: they came up to meet them: the northern tribes joined Gideon's force
decisions.reason: "They" are the men of Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, and "them" is Gideon and the men of Manasseh. "To meet" here means to come and join them, not to fight them.

decisions.choice: Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali: the tribes north of the valley
decisions.reason: These tribes lived around the valley of Jezreel and were threatened by the raiders. Zebulun and Naphtali had fought with Deborah and Barak (4:6, 10; 5:18).

decisions.choice: join
decisions.reason: "Meet" could suggest an enemy; "join" gives the sense.

decisions.choice: the tribe(s) of; Gideon and his men
decisions.reason: Readable says that the names are tribes and who "them" refers to.

records.gloss: And said Gideon to God, if you [are] delivering by my hand Israel as you have spoken,
pieces: Then Gideon said to God, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} really mean to save Israel through me, as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have said,

L.36: And Gideon said to God, "If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are going to deliver Israel by my hand, as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have said,

R.36: Then Gideon said to God, "I need to know if {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will really use me to rescue Israel, as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} said.

decisions.choice: if you are going to deliver: the sentence runs on into verse 37
decisions.reason: The condition is stated here and the test follows in the next verse: "then I will know" (verse 37). The form puts weight on whether God truly will act.

decisions.choice: by my hand: through me
decisions.reason: "Hand" means agency: God will save Israel, using Gideon as his instrument.

decisions.choice: Gideon asks again, after the sign at the rock
decisions.reason: Gideon has already been given a sign (verses 17-21) and the Spirit has come on him (verse 34), yet he asks for more. The text does not praise or blame him; God answers both requests (verses 38, 40).

decisions.choice: through me (Balanced, also verse 37); I need to know if ... (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense of "by my hand" (m2). Readable makes the condition a sentence of its own and lets verse 37 give the test.

records.source: הִנֵּ֣ה אָנֹכִ֗י מַצִּ֛יג אֶת־גִּזַּ֥ת הַצֶּ֖מֶר בַּגֹּ֑רֶן אִ֡ם טַל֩ יִהְיֶ֨ה עַֽל־הַגִּזָּ֜ה לְבַדָּ֗הּ וְעַל־כָּל־הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ חֹ֔רֶב וְיָדַעְתִּ֗י כִּֽי־תוֹשִׁ֧יעַ בְּיָדִ֛י אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּֽרְתָּ׃
records.gloss: Look, I [am] placing [the] fleece of the wool on the threshing floor. If dew is on the fleece by itself, and on all the ground dryness, then I will know that you will deliver by my hand Israel as you have spoken.
pieces: look, I am going to lay a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If dew falls on the fleece alone while all the ground stays dry, then I will be sure that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will save Israel through me, as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} said."

L.37: look, I [am] placing the fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and dryness on all the ground, then I will know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will deliver Israel by my hand, as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have said."

R.37: So I will put some wool on the floor where we beat out grain. In the morning, if there is dew only on the wool and all the ground around it is dry, then I will know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} will use me to rescue Israel, just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} said."

decisions.choice: the fleece of wool: wool shorn from a sheep in one piece
decisions.reason: A fleece is the whole coat of wool taken off a sheep at shearing. Wool soaks up moisture easily, which matters for the second test (verse 39).

decisions.choice: the threshing floor: an open, flat place for threshing grain
decisions.reason: A threshing floor was a hard, open surface, often on high ground, where dew would fall on the fleece and the ground alike. It is the open place Gideon avoided in verse 11.

decisions.choice: then I will know: the sign is something that would not happen by itself
decisions.reason: Gideon asks for dew to fall on the fleece but not on the ground around it, a difference he could see the next morning.

decisions.choice: the floor where we beat out grain; In the morning
decisions.reason: Readable explains "threshing floor" and says when Gideon would look, as verse 38 shows.

records.source: וַיְהִי־כֵ֕ן וַיַּשְׁכֵּם֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַיָּ֖זַר אֶת־הַגִּזָּ֑ה וַיִּ֤מֶץ טַל֙ מִן־הַגִּזָּ֔ה מְל֥וֹא הַסֵּ֖פֶל מָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And it was so; and he rose early on the next day and squeezed the fleece and drained dew from the fleece, [the] fullness of the bowl [of] water.
pieces: And that is what happened. When he got up early the next morning, he squeezed the fleece and wrung enough dew out of it to fill a bowl with water.

L.38: And it was so. And he rose early the next day and pressed the fleece, and he wrung dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water.

R.38: And that is what happened. Gideon got up early the next morning and squeezed the wool. So much dew came out of it that it filled a bowl with water.

decisions.choice: squeezed ... wrung out: pressed the fleece and drained the water from it
decisions.reason: The first verb means to press, the second to drain out. Gideon pressed the fleece until the dew ran out of it.

decisions.choice: a bowl full of water: a large amount
decisions.reason: The bowl is the kind of large bowl in which Jael served milk (5:25). So much water from one fleece showed that the dew had come as Gideon asked.

decisions.choice: a bowl full of water
decisions.reason: Literal smooths "the fullness of the bowl, water" into English word order.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר גִּדְעוֹן֙ אֶל־הָ֣אֱלֹהִ֔ים אַל־יִ֤חַר אַפְּךָ֙ בִּ֔י וַאֲדַבְּרָ֖ה אַ֣ךְ הַפָּ֑עַם אֲנַסֶּ֤ה נָּא־רַק־הַפַּ֨עַם֙ בַּגִּזָּ֔ה יְהִי־נָ֨א חֹ֤רֶב אֶל־הַגִּזָּה֙ לְבַדָּ֔הּ וְעַל־כָּל־הָאָ֖רֶץ יִֽהְיֶה־טָּֽל׃
records.gloss: And said Gideon to God, let not burn your anger against me, and let me speak only this time. Let me test, please, only this time with the fleece; let there be, please, dryness on the fleece by itself, and on all the ground let there be dew.
pieces: Then Gideon said to God, "Do not be angry with me, but let me speak just once more. Please let me make one more test with the fleece. This time let the fleece alone be dry, and let there be dew on all the ground."

L.39: And Gideon said to God, "Do not let {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} anger burn against me, and let me speak only this once. Let me test, please, only this once with the fleece: let it be dry on the fleece alone, and on all the ground let there be dew."

R.39: Then Gideon said to God, "Please do not be angry with me. Let me ask just one more thing. Let me test this one more time with the wool. This time let the wool be dry, and let all the ground around it be wet with dew."

decisions.choice: do not let your anger burn: do not be angry
decisions.reason: Anger is pictured as a fire that flares up (2:14, 20).

decisions.choice: let me test: Gideon knows he is asking much
decisions.reason: The verb means to put to the test. Israel was told not to test Yahweh as they did in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 6:16; Exodus 17:2, 7), and Gideon asks pardon before he does it. God grants the test without rebuke (verse 40).

decisions.choice: the reverse test: a dry fleece on wet ground
decisions.reason: Wool soaks up dew, so a wet fleece on dry ground might have a natural explanation. A dry fleece when everything around it is wet would not.

decisions.choice: just once more; one more time
decisions.reason: "Only this time" means this one further time.

decisions.choice: Do not be angry with me
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the picture, so no pronoun for God is needed.

records.gloss: And did God so in that night; and it was dry on the fleece by itself, and on all the ground there was dew.
pieces: That night God did so. Only the fleece was dry, and all the ground was covered with dew.

L.40: And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece alone, and on all the ground there was dew.

R.40: That night God did what Gideon asked. In the morning the wool was dry, but all the ground around it was wet with dew.

decisions.choice: God did so: God grants the second sign too
decisions.reason: God answers Gideon's hesitation with patience. The repeated words "dry" and "dew" from verse 39 show that everything happened exactly as Gideon asked.

decisions.choice: God: the fleece scene uses "God", not "Yahweh"
decisions.reason: In verses 36-40 the narrator and Gideon speak of "God" rather than using the name Yahweh. The same God who called Gideon (verses 14-16) answers him here.

decisions.choice: In the morning
decisions.reason: Readable adds when Gideon saw the result, as in verse 38.
